newsitem.title: USA: Solv-Ex in talks with aluminum majors.
newsitem.headline: Solv-Ex in talks with aluminum majors.

text.p: Solv-Ex Corp said it was holding talks with several leading aluminum companies regarding possible cooperation in its metal project now gathering pace in Canada.
"We are having discussions with several major companies - they are producers," Solv-Ex Corp's chairman and chief executive officer told Reuters following a company teleconference Monday.
The talks focused on what role the producers would take in Solv-Ex's aluminum project, Rendall added. He declined to name the companies but said they were from several countries.
"We are on our way in aluminum," Rendall told the teleconference. The company's alumina and aluminum projects have aroused some skepticism in the industry.
Solv-Ex will begin bitumen production from the oil sands from mid-March, with alumina and a titanium dioxide subsitute produced from allied clays from the fourth quarter.

Low cost alumina, cheap electricity at one cent per kilowatt hour from steam-driven cogeneration, and the use of non-consumable anodes in an aluminum reduction potline will produce 24,000 tonnes of aluminum metal at one third of the LME market price of $1,500 to $1,700 per tonne, Rendall said.
The non-consumable anodes have been "established as capable of working in our (aluminum reduction) cell," he added.
Dr Warren Goodenow, a former head of aluminum reduction cell development at Kaiser Aluminum has joined the company's development team, Rendall said.
Discussions were on-going to commercially test the company's aluminum reduction cells to build a 24,000 tonnes per year smelter.
"The team has now produced a feasibility study which we are examining to be able to finance the whole situation," Rendall said.
"It means an industry might well be changed," Rendall claimed.
Some two tonnes per day of alumina were needed to test three commercially sized aluminum reduction cells, Rendall said. Smelting should start the end of 1997.
"By the end of 1998 we hope to be producing 100,000 tonnes per year of alumina," Rendall said.
By the time full alumina production is reached at the end of 1998 Solv-Ex should be producing aluminum metal at the rate of 24,000 tonnes per year from the end of 1998 or early 1999, Rendall said.
About two tonnes of alumina is used to make a tonne of aluminum.
Rendall said that at the moment the alumina is for internal use only or for sale to the catalyst sector.
